title: The Dog and the Sow
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Dog and a Sow were arguing and each claimed that its own young ones were finer than those of any other animal. "Well," said the Sow at last, "mine can see, at any rate, when they come into the world: but yours are born blind."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who are the two animals arguing?
According to the passage, what does each of them claim about its own young ones?
options: That they were finer than those of any other animal
That they were the noisiest of any animal
That they grew faster than any other animal's
That they ate more than any other animal's

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who speaks last in the argument?
options: Neither, they stop arguing at the same time
A third animal who interrupts them

questions.prompt: According to the Sow, what can her young ones do as soon as they come into the world?
According to the Sow, in what condition are the Dog's young ones born?
As the passage uses it, what does "finer" mean in "finer than those of any other animal"?
Based on the passage, why does the Sow's reply settle the argument in her favor?
options: She points to a concrete fact, rather than a mere opinion, that the Dog cannot deny
She shouts louder than the Dog
She threatens the Dog with her tusks
She agrees to share the credit with the Dog

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: A demonstrable fact carries more weight than a mere boast
Sows are always wiser than dogs
Young animals should never be compared to one another

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what were the Dog and the Sow doing?
According to the passage, what word introduces the Sow's final remark?
According to the passage, what exact contrast does the Sow draw between her young and the Dog's?
options: Hers grow faster, his grow slower
Hers can see when born, his are born blind
Hers are bigger, his are smaller
Hers are louder, his are quieter

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "arguing" mean in "were arguing and each claimed"?
Based on the passage, what is implied about simply claiming your own young are "finer" without offering proof?
options: It is enough to win any argument
It carries little weight next to an actual, checkable fact
It always convinces the other animal at once
It is considered more persuasive than evidence

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Dog and a Sow both boast about their young until the Sow names a real difference in the Dog's favor
A Dog and a Sow both boast about their young until the Sow names a real difference that favors her own
A Dog and a Sow agree that their young are equally fine
A Sow admits her young are inferior to the Dog's
